title: Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)
content:
1.2 Soundness of the proposed methodology

Overall methodology: concepts, models and assumptions. FIELDWISE is built on a single organising idea that governs every methodological choice: an agricultural prediction model is only as good as its demonstrated usefulness under the conditions in which it must operate, so the methodology is designed to measure — rather than to assume — timeliness, calibration, transferability and field-level decision value. Concretely, the work reframes the object of study in four deliberate steps: from retrospective accuracy to prospective prediction, then to transferability, and finally to field-level decision value. This reframing is operationalised as a four-stage validation ladder that structures the whole action — Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem for scientific development and validation, then Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив for cross-country transferability, then the AgroVIR farmer field for operational transferability, and finally the DrR Web MVP for research-to-operation delivery. Each rung is a genuine test that the model can fail, and the design is arranged so that a failure is quantified rather than concealed.

The methodology rests on a small number of explicit concepts, models and assumptions, each tied to a falsifiable hypothesis so that the underpinning assumptions are checkable rather than implicit. First, water stress is defined physiologically rather than through vegetation-index proxies (the assumption behind H1: soil-water availability and atmospheric demand combined with hyperspectral crop-response information will flag developing stress before substantial canopy greenness deterioration). Second, high-information proximal hyperspectral signatures are assumed to be partially reconstructable at Sentinel-2 resolution (H2), and the model that realises this is a concrete transfer pipeline: spectral-response-function resampling, concurrent proximal/satellite observation, and scale-aware calibration, producing a Sentinel-compatible feature library. Third, prediction is treated as a prospective, uncertainty-aware forecasting problem: the modelling programme spans transparent baseline models, Random Forest/XGBoost models and Bayesian/hierarchical models, with multi-horizon forecasting and explicit probability calibration and uncertainty quantification, so that forecasts are issued at actionable horizons with stated confidence rather than as point estimates. Fourth, generalisation is assumed to be the true measure of quality, so a leakage-safe validation design is fixed at the outset (WP1 Historical Data and Target Design), enforced by leave-one-year-out validation and an explicit zero-shot Hungary-to-Bulgaria transfer test (WP4 Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability). Fifth, usefulness is assumed to be distinct from accuracy, so Field Decision Value (FDV) is introduced as a final evaluation layer, and warning lead time is made a primary model-selection criterion (H6). The data foundation is not speculative: the source domain is an approximately five-year historical soil-plant-atmosphere archive from Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem, and the model crop is processing tomato, a demanding predictive-irrigation system in which productivity depends strongly on the temporal interaction of water availability, atmospheric demand, developmental stage and irrigation management.

How the methodology delivers the objectives. The design maps each objective onto a work package whose method produces the objective's measurable output. WP1 Historical Data and Target Design harmonises the archive and fixes the physiological target and the leakage-safe split, delivering the harmonised database (D1.1 Harmonised historical database, month 6) and the protocol that binds all later validation (D1.2 Data/target/validation protocol, month 6), serving O1. WP2 Physiological Early Warning and Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel Transfer executes the discovery-and-scaling pipeline for O2. WP3 Prospective and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction builds and benchmarks the forecasting models for O3, culminating in the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2). WP4 Temporal and Cross-Country Transferability runs the temporal and geographic transfer experiments and the adaptation study for O4. WP5 Operational Transfer, Decision Value and Web MVP carries the model to commercial fields, quantifies operational transferability and decision value, and delivers the web MVP, serving O5 and O6. The inter-work-package data dependencies (WP1 feeds WP2 and WP3; WP2 feeds WP3; WP3 feeds WP4 and WP5; WP4 feeds WP5) make the sequence a single evidential chain rather than a set of parallel studies, so each objective is reached on validated inputs from the one before it.

Challenges in the chosen methodology and how they are overcome. The methodology's principal risks are identified explicitly and each carries a matched mitigation, and — distinctively — the design treats several of the hardest outcomes as scientific findings rather than as failures. Where the historical MATE information may be incomplete, the approach uses a common-data subset, quality flags and prospective augmentation. Where a hyperspectral index has no Sentinel equivalent, or a spectral-domain or proximal/satellite spatial mismatch arises, the mitigations are to retain such indices for physiological discovery while excluding them from the operational Sentinel model, to apply spectral-response-function resampling with concurrent-sensor comparison, and to aggregate to representative plots/zones. Where too few physiological stress events occur, targeted temporal sampling across stress gradients is used; where cloud gaps threaten optical coverage, temporal windows and Sentinel-1 are used where scientifically useful. The generalisation risks are the ones the project is built to measure: an unseen-year performance drop is an expected scientific outcome to be quantified and adapted to; a Hungary-to-Bulgaria drop is countered with limited local and Bayesian adaptation; a farmer-field drop is quantified as the operational gap, with inputs and model simplified where necessary. If the Bayesian approach does not outperform simpler machine learning, the simpler model is retained where it is superior in calibration or FDV; if a prediction is accurate but too late, lead time governs model selection; and if full AgroVIR integration proves infeasible, the MVP assessment plus an integration roadmap remain a successful endpoint. The explicit risk philosophy is that failure of zero-shot transfer is not project failure — establishing that a MATE-trained model cannot reliably transfer to Bulgaria without a defined amount of local calibration is itself a significant scientific finding. This converts methodological risk into methodological information.

Integration of methods and disciplines to pursue the objectives. An interdisciplinary approach is not optional here; it is the precondition for the objectives, because the central problem lives precisely at the boundary between plant biology and geospatial data science. The methodology therefore integrates four disciplinary strands and assigns each a concrete role in the evidential chain. Crop physiology, agronomy and plant protection supply the physiologically meaningful stress definition and the field experimentation that make H1 testable; this expertise is carried by the fellow, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, a plant physiologist. Geoinformatics, Earth-observation time-series analysis and hyperspectral/field spectroscopy supply the sensor-domain transfer methods (H2) and the satellite-scaling design; this is the expertise of the host, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), and of the supervisor, Prof. András Jung, whose field is remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy. Machine learning and Bayesian/hierarchical meta-modelling supply the prospective, uncertainty-aware prediction and the adaptation methods for cross-country transfer; this is the domain of the co-supervisor, Dr. Roland Hollós, who provides the methodological lead and quality assurance for model development and testing. Research-software engineering and operational evaluation supply the translation from validated model to web MVP and the commercial-field decision-value assessment, with the non-academic placement at AgroVIR embedding the operational strand inside a company that runs commercial farms. The integration is explicitly two-way: the host transfers geoinformatics, EO time-series analysis, hyperspectral-to-multispectral transfer, spatio-temporal and Bayesian hierarchical modelling, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning/domain adaptation and reproducible geospatial computation to the fellow, while the fellow transfers plant physiology, horticultural crop science, water-stress experimentation, physiological phenotyping, hyperspectral field measurement and the biological interpretation of EO to the host. Methodologically, this bidirectional transfer is what allows spectral observations to be anchored to physiological meaning and machine-learned relationships to be interpreted as crop-water processes rather than as black-box correlations — it is the mechanism, not merely a benefit, of the physiological-target and transferability objectives. The consortium is configured so that each discipline owns the environment its methods need: Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem provides the experimental environment and primary scientific validation, Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив provides an independent, contrasting-country processing-tomato environment for the cross-country test, and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság provides the commercial farmer-field bridge, together forming an academic-research-industry knowledge chain.

Gender dimension and other diversity aspects in the research content. The planned research and innovation content concerns the crop physiology of processing tomato, proximal and satellite spectral sensing, and the statistical and machine-learning modelling of crop water stress; it involves no human or animal biological subjects whose sex or gender is an analytical variable. A biological sex/gender dimension in the research content is therefore not relevant to FIELDWISE, and this is stated as a reasoned justification rather than an omission, in line with the question's scope (which concerns the content of the research, not the gender balance of the team). Diversity is, however, methodologically central to the project in the form that is relevant to it: agro-environmental and operational diversity is the explicit object of study. The validation ladder is deliberately built to span diversity of agro-climate and management — a Hungarian research environment versus a contrasting Bulgarian one, and controlled research fields versus heterogeneous farmer-managed commercial fields — precisely so that the model is tested against, rather than sheltered from, the variability of real production settings; identifying universal versus site-specific predictors is an explicit WP4 task. Where the research does engage people, it does so inclusively and with safeguards: the operational assessment gathers structured feedback from AgroVIR staff and participating commercial growers under informed consent and a right of withdrawal, with no health, biometric or special-category data collected, and commercially sensitive farm data handled under a data-sharing agreement with results published only in aggregated or anonymised form. End-user engagement with a diverse population of commercial growers is thus part of the method by which operational transferability and decision value are assessed.

Open science practices as an integral part of the methodology. Open science is embedded in the methodology rather than appended to it, following the principle "as open as possible, as closed as necessary". Because the scientific contribution of FIELDWISE is a way of validating and transferring agricultural models, its most important open outputs are methodological and reproducibility artefacts: harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, the hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, analysis and model code where intellectual property permits, model cards (the FIELDWISE predictive engine is delivered with a model card, D3.2), FAIR metadata, selected derived/anonymised datasets, and open-access publications. Publishing the leakage-safe validation design and the validation split manifests is itself a methodological safeguard, because it exposes exactly the train/test separation that guards against the optimistic in-sample scoring the project sets out to overcome, making the transferability claims independently checkable. FAIR data management is applied throughout, and a Data Management Plan will be delivered as a project deliverable by month 6, consistent with the instrument's requirement that training foster an Open Science culture and good scientific conduct; the plan governs which datasets are opened, the anonymisation and aggregation applied to commercially sensitive AgroVIR farm data, and the retention and lawful-basis terms for the personal data held by the web MVP, with ELTE's Data Protection Officer consulted before the first user account is created. Open science and FAIR practice, together with generative-AI literacy and research integrity, are also carried as transferable-skill strands of the Career Development Plan, so the fellow's open-science competence is trained and evidenced, not merely asserted. In sum, the methodology is sound because its concepts and assumptions are made explicit and falsifiable, its models are matched to the prediction task and its uncertainty made visible, its interdisciplinary integration is the mechanism by which the objectives are reached, its diversity is the agro-environmental and operational variability it deliberately tests against, and its open-science and data-management practices are woven into the same reproducibility design that its scientific claims depend on.

claim_statuses.claim_summary: The methodology is organised as a four-stage validation ladder: MATE (scientific development and validation) -> MVCRI (cross-country transferability) -> AgroVIR farmer field (operational transferability) -> DrR Web MVP (research-to-operation delivery), reframing accuracy -> prospective prediction -> transferability -> decision value.

Water stress is defined physiologically rather than via vegetation-index proxies, with early-warning based on soil-water availability, atmospheric demand and hyperspectral crop response before canopy greenness deterioration (H1).

Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer uses spectral-response-function resampling, concurrent proximal/satellite observation and scale-aware calibration to produce a Sentinel-compatible feature library (H2).

Prediction is prospective and uncertainty-aware, spanning transparent baselines, Random Forest/XGBoost and Bayesian/hierarchical models, with multi-horizon forecasting and probability calibration/uncertainty quantification.
A leakage-safe validation design is fixed in WP1 and enforced by leave-one-year-out validation and an explicit zero-shot Hungary-to-Bulgaria (MATE->MVCRI) transfer test in WP4.
Field Decision Value (FDV) is introduced as a final evaluation layer and warning lead time is a primary model-selection criterion (H6).
Each objective O1-O6 maps to a named work package producing its measurable output, with WP titles and deliverables (D1.1, D1.2 at month 6; D3.2) reproduced from the canonical reference pack.
Inter-work-package data dependencies (WP1->WP2/WP3; WP2->WP3; WP3->WP4/WP5; WP4->WP5) form a single evidential chain.

Methodological challenges are identified as risks R01-R13 with matched mitigations, and the risk philosophy treats failed zero-shot transfer as a significant scientific finding rather than project failure.

The approach is interdisciplinary by necessity, integrating crop physiology/agronomy, geoinformatics/Earth observation, machine learning/Bayesian modelling and research-software/operational evaluation.

Knowledge transfer is bidirectional (ELTE geoinformatics/EO/Bayesian methods to fellow; fellow plant physiology/agronomy/hyperspectral field measurement to ELTE), forming an academic-research-industry chain across ELTE, MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR.

Spine identities: fellow Dr. Rositsa Cholakova (plant physiologist), host Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), supervisor Prof. András Jung (remote sensing/hyperspectral), co-supervisor Dr. Roland Hollós (ML/meta-modelling, methodological lead for model development and testing).

The consortium partners each own the environment their discipline requires: MATE (experimental/data environment and primary validation), MVCRI (independent contrasting-country environment), AgroVIR (commercial farmer-field bridge and non-academic placement host).

A biological sex/gender dimension is not relevant to the research content because it concerns crop physiology, spectral sensing and ML with no human or animal biological subjects; stated as a reasoned justification.

Diversity relevant to the project is agro-environmental and operational (Hungary vs Bulgaria; research vs commercial fields; identifying universal vs site-specific predictors) and is deliberately spanned by the validation ladder.

End-user engagement gathers structured feedback from AgroVIR staff and commercial growers under informed consent with right of withdrawal, no special-category data, and commercially sensitive farm data handled under a data-sharing agreement with aggregated/anonymised publication.

Open science follows 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary', with open outputs including harmonisation protocols, validation split manifests, hyperspectral-to-Sentinel methodology, code where IP permits, model cards, FAIR metadata, anonymised datasets and open-access publications.
A Data Management Plan will be delivered as a project deliverable by month 6, consistent with the instrument's Open Science training requirement.
Open science and FAIR practice, generative-AI literacy and research integrity are carried as transferable-skill strands of the Career Development Plan.
The source-domain data is an approximately five-year historical soil-plant-atmosphere / hyperspectral archive from MATE and the model crop is processing tomato.
ELTE's Data Protection Officer is consulted before the first web MVP user account is created, covering lawful basis, retention and data minimisation for farm contact details and field boundaries.
